summary: Defines enhancements to the OSPF routing protocol so it can work efficiently over demand circuits, such as dial-up or pay-per-use links, which would otherwise be kept busy or brought up by routine OSPF traffic. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1793 adapts OSPF for links that cost money or resources while they are open. It suppresses routine messages after routers synchronize and avoids sending refreshes that do not change routing information.

questions: how does ospf work over demand circuits
what is ospf demand circuit support
what is the ospf donotage bit
how are ospf hellos suppressed on demand circuits
when does ospf suppress demand circuit hellos
subtitle: How OSPF reduces routine traffic on links that cost money or resources to keep open.

tldr.problem: OSPF's routine Hellos and link-state refreshes can keep dial-up and other usage-charged connections open.
tldr.mechanism: Routers use the DC-bit to indicate support, mark selected LSAs DoNotAge, flood only real changes over eligible demand circuits, and suppress Hellos after synchronization on point-to-point links.
tldr.outcome: The data-link connection can close when it has no traffic, but periodic refresh protection is lost. RFC 1793 is updated by RFC 3883.

today: RFC 1793 is a Proposed Standard published in April 1995 and is updated by RFC 3883.

sections.title: The Demand Circuit Model
sections.content:
A demand circuit is a network segment whose cost depends on connection time, transmitted bytes or packets, or both. Examples include ISDN, X.25 switched virtual circuits, and dial-up lines.

When there is no routing or application data, the data-link connection can remain closed. OSPF assumes the circuit is available unless it receives evidence that it cannot be opened.
sections.plainLanguage: A demand circuit may cost more while it is connected or carrying traffic. The design aims to keep it closed when there is no data to send.

sections.title: The DC-bit and DoNotAge
sections.content:
A router sets the DC-bit in its originated LSAs to show that it can process DoNotAge LSAs. The high bit of the 16-bit LS age field is the DoNotAge bit, with value 0x8000; an LSA carrying it does not age in the link-state database.

DoNotAge LSAs can remain after their originator disappears. A router flushes one only after it has been in the database for at least MaxAge and the originator has been unreachable for at least MaxAge.
sections.plainLanguage: The DC-bit signals that a router understands LSAs that do not age in storage. A separate rule removes an old such LSA after its originator has been unreachable long enough.

sections.title: Interoperating with Older Routers
sections.content:
An unmodified OSPF router may treat a DoNotAge LSA as if it had reached MaxAge. To avoid incompatible LSAs, they are allowed in an area only when every LSA in that area's database has the DC-bit set.

If an LSA without the DC-bit appears, routers flush DoNotAge LSAs and their originators reissue them without the bit. Area border routers use indication-LSAs to signal support limitations across regular area boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use the DC-bit to check that every router in an area can understand DoNotAge LSAs. If one cannot, the area returns to ordinary aging for those advertisements.

sections.title: Negotiating Hello Suppression
sections.content:
On a point-to-point demand circuit, routers set the DC-bit in Hellos and Database Description packets to negotiate Hello suppression. If the neighbor indicates it does not agree, periodic Hellos continue.

After database synchronization reaches Full, Hellos stop. If the neighbor is later judged unavailable, it returns to Down and the router sends Hellos at PollInterval while it tries to synchronize again. Broadcast and NBMA networks still need periodic Hellos for their normal operation.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers exchange Hellos until they agree that both can suppress them and their databases are synchronized. If the neighbor becomes unavailable, periodic checks resume.

sections.title: Flooding Changed Information
sections.content:
Demand-circuit flooding changes apply only when every LSA in the area's database indicates DoNotAge support. In that case, routers send only LSAs whose contents changed over demand circuits; a refresh that changes only sequence number and checksum is not sent over that circuit.

When a changed LSA is sent over a demand circuit, its copy has DoNotAge set unless its age is MaxAge. A separate flooding-algorithm change applies on all interfaces: a router responds to an older LSA with its current copy, rather than acknowledging the older instance.
sections.plainLanguage: Over an eligible demand circuit, OSPF sends routing information only when its contents change. It marks the transmitted copy so a receiver does not need routine refreshes.

sections.title: Costs and Limitations
sections.content:
Removing periodic refreshes reduces protection against LSAs being lost or corrupted in a router's database. Database checksum sums also cannot verify synchronization in the usual way because LSA sequence numbers can differ across demand circuits.

The RFC recommends isolating demand circuits in stub areas or NSSAs where possible. Oversubscription, where a router cannot open all its circuits, can delay topology updates. The RFC does not discuss security issues.
sections.plainLanguage: Less routine traffic saves connection cost, but it also removes some checks on stored routing information. A router that lacks enough open connections may not learn about a change promptly.
